thread.title: Investing Beyond Flash And DRAM - Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC)

author: Stephen Breezy
title: Investing Beyond Flash And DRAM - Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC)
text:
Two long years ago, I penned a piece entitled, " Intel Has No Plans For 10 Nanometer Chips ". This drew the regular response from the ever-present Statler and Waldorf types that seem to be very much at home here on the Internet. As usual, none of the responses included the premise that perhaps I was correct.
Fast-forward to present and, instead of a harebrained idea, Intel ( INTC ) is now synonymous with its failure to execute at 10 nanometers. And, yet, I received no credit.
Is This Thing On? I've rambled ad nauseam about the priceless nature of the non-silicon switching technology that is present in 3D XPoint/Optane chips. I won't repeat this in detail because, like the 10 nanometer prediction, it is just simply too much for most to fathom until, of course, it happens. In the interim, realize that, this whole time, my only point was that it didn't make sense for Intel to release the disruptive iterations of this technology until it secured its exclusive rights - a subset of which that are either shared with or outright owned by Micron ( MU ) which, in turn, "might not be sympathetic to Intel".
As suspected, they aren't.
Leveraging the hybrid wisdom of Bob Seger and Donald Rumsfeld, we know more now what we didn't know then but there are still unknowns of all variety. Notably, we now know that Micron will exercise its option to purchase Intel's half of IMFT. We also know that Intel and Micron have announced their intentions to go their own ways with respect to development of XPoint.
This is a very important point: management at both Micron and Intel believe that 3D XPoint is viable enough to pursue independently. This outcome was likely a fiduciary responsibility - not an actual decision. Nonetheless, we can surmise that they are operating with information that we do not have. When all of the pundits characterize Optane as a stillborn technology, realize that they said the same thing about the silicon transistor during its development - "this is the way that we've always done it". Never mind the man behind the curtain.
But it isn't what you know More importantly, we know that Intel recently filed suit against Doyle Rivers , a former employee who "secretly" accepted a job at Micron. In the complaint, Intel's attorneys provide hints as to the sensational nature of the underlying 3D XPoint technology:
Rivers is a computer hardware engineer who was involved in Intel's development of 3D XPoint, a revolutionary new type of memory technology in which Intel has invested over a billion dollars. [...] In September 2018, Rivers secretly accepted an engineering position with Micron and then, as he prepared to leave Intel for that job, engaged in a covert and calculated effort to collect Intel's confidential, proprietary, and trade secret technical and personnel information. [...] Only a few hundred people in the world have specialized knowledge pertaining to 3D XPoint, and the processes for developing and manufacturing 3D XPoint are not written in any textbook or taught in any school. Intel is informed and believes and therefore alleges that having access to the Intel Trade Secrets-including a list containing the few hundred individuals in the world qualified to work on 3D XPoint - gave Rivers and his new employer an unfair advantage in their effort to compete with Intel in the marketplace and could allow Rivers and his new employer to develop and productize 3D XPoint more quickly than would have been possible had they started from scratch.
Inspection of the patents on which Mr. Rivers is listed as an inventor reveals that most of his work is assigned to Micron with only a smattering assigned to Intel. To quote myself from a 2015 article :
But Intel isn't holding all of the sexy intellectual property for themselves as they seem to have a good understanding that Micron deals with the fabrication side of the equation even though some Micron patents hold Intel inventors.
So we also know that there had been an open door policy for Rivers to work between the companies - a door that is now closed only subsequent to Micron's public demeanor to take the IMFT ball and go home. For some reason (and I suspect that there are many, many billions of those), now there is a distinction. It is unfortunate how money can change relationships.
Out riding fences So, in September, Micron allegedly recruited Rivers. In October, the company announced its intent to call Intel's share of IMFT . Intel then countered with the Rivers suit at the end of November. But the suit names only Rivers - not Micron. If you add up all of the "knowns", it sure looks to me like Intel is getting desperate and the suit is just an artifact of that desperation.
But there are a lot of unknowns here. Rivers, for example, might be an Intel mole. Why did he have access to personnel information? That's seems mighty sloppy or perhaps all too convenient. Regardless, I don't think that it buys any time at this point - there's just too much at stake here. For those who don't wish to sift through my previous manifestos, the major takeaways are as follows:
The fab-integrated Ovonic threshold switches present in 3D XPoint also have the capability to replace SRAM and DRAM in three dimensions. Using language from Intel's patent : Thus, comparing volatile memories, the speed of some embodiments of the present invention may be comparable to that of a six transistor static random access memory, but the size of some embodiments of the present invention, using only a single transistor and an ovonic threshold switch, may be considerably smaller than that of standard six transistor static random access memory. Thus, some embodiments of the present invention may provide a volatile memory with comparable speed at much smaller size.
This new type of volatile memory combines the density of DRAM with the speed of SRAM and facilitates very high-speed, high-density memory with infinite durability to be fabricated over the top of the CPU logic using Micron's existing " CMOS under Array " technology. Except now you have a processor under the main memory on a single chip - very high-speed, very low-power and very cheap to manufacture. As Intel's Rick Coulson outlined, with "fast enough" paging memory (read: Optane gen1 already meets the requirement), you no longer need DRAM. 3D XPoint gen2 will likely include new materials (substituting indium for germanium is the key takeaway from the patents) that will provide the ground-shaking improvements in performance, power and price. Exclusive ownership of this technology would allow Intel to dominate all processor markets (CPU, GPU, AI, mobile - everything). Even a small head start would be worth a phenomenal sum and certainly a good reason to delay their 10 nanometer products for some years. Since they will soon be obsolete, it would be clever to leak flash and DRAM manufacturing technology to would-be competitors. You know - let them spend $50 billion in the fight before letting them know that you're not left handed . Doubt is not a pleasant condition Years ago, as Micron's share price ventured down into the single digits, I surmised that the stock was worth $60/share based on the value of its 3D XPoint technology. When the share price reached this figure over the summer, I did cash-in, and I used the proceeds to short the broader market (which was only a hunch based on probability).
When that panned out as the certainty on IMFT's future was materializing, I decided to flip the investment back around. I've been very fortunate on timing of everything. With the new year, new facts, and new Micron street price upon us, loving Micron at these levels is easy. Its IMFT call option timeline is detailed as follows :
The IMFT joint venture agreement extends through 2024 and includes certain buy-sell rights. At any time through December 2018, Intel can put to us, and from January 2019 through December 2021, we can call from Intel, Intel's interest in IMFT, in either case, for a price that approximates Intel's interest in the net book value of IMFT plus member debt at the time of the closing. If Intel exercises its put right, we can elect to set the closing date of the transaction any time between six months and two years following such election by Intel and we can elect to receive financing of the purchase price from Intel for one to two years from the closing date. If we exercise our call right, Intel can elect to set the closing date of the transaction to be any time between six months and one year following such election. Following the closing date resulting from exercise of either the put or the call, we will continue to supply to Intel for a period of one year between 50% and 100%, at Intel's choice, of Intel's immediately preceding six-month period pre-closing volumes of IMFT products for the first six-month period following the closing and between 0% and 100%, at Intel's choice, of Intel's first six-month period following the closing volumes of IMFT products for the second six-month period following the closing, at a margin that varies depending on whether the put or call was exercised.
Summary The clock is now ticking on an once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Micron, which heavily includes its shareholders. I expect soon to hear Micron's announcement of the details of its IMFT call option so that it can get the party started. 3D XPoint gen1 isn't really worth a hill of beans right now because it requires a completely new processor architecture in order to be beneficial. And Micron doesn't have processor tech in-house.
Intel's delay in its 10 nanometer products appears to be intentional to this end - it behooves it to keep everything a secret until it's secured it for itself. With the most recent developments, I suspect that not only is the cat out of the bag, but also Micron has already won by another suitor, with the Doyle Rivers complaint being evidence of this last-ditch effort.
The three-dimensional, non-silicon switching technology in 3D XPoint is a national treasure. As such, it will remain under US ownership . While that restricts Micron's potential suitors, the list is still very impressive. Besides Intel, I expect to see Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) all bidding for a chance to own the future. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ) will need to sit on the sidelines with Intel as the bigger players fight for Micron. It is also possible that Micron could remain independent and sub-license the 3D XPoint tech to the whole lot.
Depending on how the Rivers suit plays out, I expect to see Micron's IMFT call play out over the next year, give or take. I have no idea what is in the broader economic cards at this point, but a falling tide could add some drama.
Disclosure: I am/we are long MU.
